blocks.cap: Obon lanterns in a Kita lane after dark

blocks.p: Rei walked home from the roof in the dark. The heat had not gone down with the sun. It sat in the narrow streets of Kita like water in a bath that nobody had drained. The cicadas had stopped for the night, and in their place there was the hum of air conditioners on every balcony, dripping onto the pavement below. Paper lanterns hung outside some of the houses for Obon, white and pale blue, each with a family name brushed on the side. A few of them had candles inside. Most had small electric bulbs now, and one of the bulbs was flickering in a way that had nothing to do with the wiring.

He passed a konbini on the corner, bright as an aquarium. A delivery man was asleep in his van outside it with the engine running for the cool air and his mouth open. Inside, a girl in a striped uniform was stacking rice balls into the fridge, very slowly, as if the night would never end. An old woman came out with a bag of peaches and a bunch of chrysanthemums for a family altar. She stopped at the door and looked back over her shoulder at the empty street, the way people in Kita had been doing all month. Then she shook her head at herself and went on. Rei climbed the stairs to the flat. The stairwell smelled of the neighbour's cigarettes, as it always did. He let himself in and did not turn on the light.

There is no stair to the Axis. That was the first true thing Rei learned about it. He had pictured something without quite admitting it. A door in a sub-basement. A vault in a ward-house. A secret the CVD kept behind a grade he did not have. There was nothing like that. The Axis was not under Tokyo the way a basement is under a house. It was under Tokyo the way meaning is under the words of a sentence. It was in every part of the thing, and there was no single spot he could point to.

So he did not go down to reach it. He sat on the kitchen floor with his back against the cupboard and Gin's book closed in his lap, and he let both of his paths open at once. The first of Rei's was Clairsentience, the searching, sensing one, which he had always half allowed himself. The second lay beneath it. He had never named it. He had spent his whole life holding it flat, because Gin had taught him to, at this same table, before he could even read. Now he let them both come up. He let the city stop being a place. For as long as he could stand it, he let it become a structure. The structure had a floor, and the floor was the Axis. He was standing on it. He had been standing on it all his life.

His sight went further than any word he had for it. The walls of the flat did not disappear. They went clear, like glass. The veil itself, the thin wall between the living and the dead, stood up out of the city like a building made of light. He could see every thick part and every thin part, every line where it was under strain. He could see where it was being held, and where it was being pulled. Kurosawa had once called this the city becoming transparent. Not invisible. Transparent. Gin's book put it on the last line of the sight scale, the line Gin himself had never reached. Under it Gin had written three words. No off switch. Rei understood them now. He could not have closed this sight if he had wanted to. He could only hold on and look.

It cost him at once, and it cost him the thing he had least of, which was his hold on his own mind. The madness came up through his open paths like water through a hole in a boat. It did not come as fear. It came as recognition. It was the terrible feeling of finally seeing the room he had always been in. Under everything there was a direction. It was not a place. It was a slope, and it grew steeper the longer he faced it. It was warm. And it was paying attention to him. It knew he was looking. Every ability he had ever used had come up out of that slope, and the slope had noticed, every time.

This was the Font. Gin's book had explained it as the source, the deep place every gift comes from and every dead soul finally flows back into. Rei knew it now the way he would have known the sea. Gin's last chapter had put it carefully. Aware that you are accessing it. Gin had not said what it felt like to stand at the top of the slope and want to go down. It felt like coming home. That was the danger the book had underlined twice. The souls that go all the way down dissolve into it completely, and they do not feel it as dying. They feel it as arriving. So the part of Rei that wanted to go on living had to hold on, with both hands, to one plain fact. The feeling of home was the trap. It was not the truth. The wanting was only a feeling. It was not a direction to follow.
He held on. And because he held on, he could see which way the slope ran.

blocks.cap: Shinjuku, where every CVD map puts the city's source point

blocks.p: It did not run toward Shinjuku. Every CVD map he had ever seen put the city's source point under Shinjuku, the busiest crossing of grief and money in Japan. The slope did not care about the maps. It ran north, into Kita. And it reached its lowest point in a place he knew. Three hundred metres northeast of the kitchen he was sitting in. A few streets of shuttered shops, a short walk from this flat.

He almost laughed. It came out as a breath. Gin had chosen this flat, and Rei had never understood why. It was cramped. The heater broke every winter. The stairwell smelled of the neighbour's cigarettes. And Gin had signed for it in a week without looking at anything else. Now Rei knew. Gin's Clairsentience had turned toward this warmth the way a plant turns toward a window, years before Gin knew what he was feeling. He had moved them both to the edge of the Font because it had felt like the right place to sleep. Everything that had happened since had happened three hundred metres from the centre of everything.

Now he could see the lattice, the great frame that held the veil in place. It ran under the whole city. It was made of thirteen places, set around the slope like the spokes of a wheel around its hub. Twelve of them were occupied. He felt each one the way he would feel eyes in a dark room. Each place was a pressure with a name he almost knew, and each pressure had a person in it. They were small and warm and very far apart, and they felt, strangely, like people. Grief. Rage. Love. Fear. Wonder. Despair. Joy. Shame. Hunger. Courage. Longing. Awe. Twelve emotions, and each one ran through a single living person, so that it kept moving and never settled on the city to rot. These were the Thirteen, the holders the old records spoke of. Their seats were not thrones. They were load-bearing, like pillars under a roof. The whole careful weave of them was the wall. It was the veil itself, a breath the city was holding.

Under the lattice, very faint, lay a second one in the same shape. It had thirteen hollow places, dark ones, each cut to fit one of the twelve, and one cut to fit the thirteenth. These were the demon shells, the dark twin of the living holders. Rei did not look at them for long. He felt enough to know that the dark places wanted the light ones. And he felt that one of them, the one called Despair, was pressed so hard against its living twin that he could barely tell the two apart.

blocks.cap: The figure at the hub of the lattice, holding the wall shut

blocks.p: At the hub, where all thirteen spokes met and the slope ran down into nothing, there was a figure. It stood in a light so cold and so complete that Rei's eyes watered, even though he was not seeing with his eyes. It had its back to him. It had its back to the whole world. All of its attention was on the wall, and it was holding something shut. Rei could not see its face. He did not think anyone could. But it was shaped like a man. Not a god, not a machine, not a storm. A man, standing very still, the way a person stands when he has been carrying something heavy for so long that he no longer notices his arms.

Every path was lit in him. Rei had never felt all six at once. He had not known it could be done. Clairsentience and Telepathy. Telekinesis and Psychometabolism. Psychokinesis and Teleportation. Every one of them was open to its limit. And through him ran all thirteen spokes, every register from Grief to Duty, alive in one place at the same moment. Rei understood, in a rush that hurt, what the last row of the rank table in Gin's book had meant. X. Axis. Was human. Is no longer. This was what a human being looked like from the outside, once he had become the centre. The Font was not a well that happened to hold him. The Font was what poured out of him.

Rei wanted to call out to him. He did not. Gin's book had told him that much. It answers one question per approach. It does not show its face. It returns the practitioner. And it answered only those who had come all the way in. Rei was not in. He was looking down a well from the kitchen floor.
And the thirteenth place was empty. The emptiness had a shape, and the shape was a wound.

He made himself look at the empty place. The lattice felt him looking, the way still water feels a dropped stone, and it showed him its history. It did not use words. The Axis had no use for words. It showed him the way a scar remembers the knife.

The thirteenth spoke was Duty. The CVD had never named it right. On its forms it was Register XIII, unclassified, and its instruments read the stillness there as nothing at all. Null-emotive. But it was not empty. It was full. Duty was what obligation becomes when it has been the only thing for so long that nothing remains that remembers a time before it. The man at the hub had sat in that chair first, long ago, and he had never fully stood up. Living holders had come and gone beside him. The last of them had died in 2009. When a holder dies, the weight passes to someone close by with the right shape of gift, and in 2009 no such person had been standing near enough. So the chair had read as vacant ever since. It was not truly vacant. The man at the centre had reached out and taken Duty into his own hands, on top of everything else he held. He had carried it alone for six years. He could not keep doing it. He was leaning. And the place where the lean was worst, where the lattice was spending the most of itself to hold the gap shut, was the seam under Kita.

The empty chair and the thinning wall were not two problems. They were one wound, seen from two ends. Kita had been going wrong since the year the chair emptied. The great wave of deaths in 2011 had pushed it further. And the thing that had taken Rei's brother had spent a month walking the city, pressing on the bruise.

Kneeling there, on the floor that was the underside of meaning, he understood why a Duty demon would want this seat above any other. Kurosawa had given him the word in the cold room, and the Healer had given him every reason since. The Healer did not want power over the living. Rei had been wrong about that from the first morning in the kitchen, and the mistake had nearly cost him everything. It wanted the office. Under the lattice of the living, in the matching dark place cut to the shape of Duty, there was a chair for its own kind, and it wanted to sit there. It wanted to rule the far side of the wall, beside the few demons it trusted. It wanted to finish the duty that death had interrupted for it forty years ago. It was completely sincere. That sincerity was the most dangerous thing in the whole structure. A monster can be fought. A martyr cannot. And the thing wearing his brother believed, all the way down, that it was the only mercy left.

But Rei saw the lie folded inside the sincerity. It was small and it was absolute, like the tremble he had once seen in the old man's dish. To take that seat, the Healer had to finish tearing the wall. It could not climb into the chair while the lattice was still spending itself to hold the gap. The wall had to go fully thin. The held breath had to go all the way out. And for the one hour it would take a new occupant to climb in and take the weight, the door would stand open in both directions. Whatever came through that door, while the Healer was busy becoming a law, would not be the Healer's problem. It would be the problem of every living thing in Kita. The mercy was real. But the mercy needed a flood. And the demon had made its peace with the flood. To a thing built for duty, drowning a district so that it could take its seat correctly was not a price. It was a small number rounded away.
He felt both demons move toward the wound from opposite sides. The feeling was the worst kind of proof, the kind that ends the comfort of not being sure.

Kishin came the way weather comes. Kishin was the Despair demon. It was wearing Fukai Rinka, the woman the Far-Shore Circle called Kanna-sensei, and it spoke through Kaito, the hollowed young courier who preached in the drained pool. But the demon itself did not walk toward the seam. The seam began to walk toward it. The scored places pulled open along the lines Kishin had spent the whole season tearing. It was turning itself inside out as it came. Rei saw what it was becoming, and his stomach dropped. The man at the hub held every register in a light too cold to look at. Kishin was growing the same shape in the dark, from the hollow places upward. A dark mirror of the Axis. An inverted god. It did not want the empty chair. It wanted the wall gone, and the dark lattice raised on this side of it, the living side, with itself at the top. It wanted to rule the city Rei lived in. And it, too, believed this was healing. The Axis was full of sincere disasters tonight.

The Healer came the way an appointment comes. Patient, expected, prepared. It was being carried toward the seam in Gin's tired body through the festival nights, calm and unhurried, like a thing that has done the hard part and only needs to arrive. The two demons were not allies. They had never spoken. They did not need to. Kishin would tear the wall down because it hungered for the living side. The Healer would step through the torn wall into its chair out of duty. Each one's disaster was the other one's first step. But under the Healer's calm Rei felt something else, cold as a scalpel. The Healer did not mean to leave Kishin standing once the work was done. Kishin meant to rule this side, and the Healer wanted it dead before it could. A demon can only be killed on this side from inside a body. That was one more reason the Healer had kept Gin's body so carefully, so gently, in such good repair.

Rei was the only mind at the Axis that simply wanted the wall to hold. He had no seat, no grade, no law. He had two paths he could not keep open without drowning. And he had a brother somewhere inside the appointment, still tapping.

From down here, the coming nights did not look like a question with an answer. They looked like the kitchen at 3:47 in the morning, with every door standing open, and behind each door something he loved, waiting to be paid for. He saw the Healer in its chair and Kita under water. He saw himself at the wound, both hands on it, and nothing left behind his eyes. He saw Gin's hand in his, the two of them running, and the lanterns going out behind them street by street. He made himself stop looking. The structure had no opinion about which door he chose. It only knew that every door cost something.

The slope pulled at him, warm and patient. For one long second he leaned toward it. Then he did the only thing Gin's book had told him to do with the wanting. He did not follow it. He shut the second path first, the nameless one, the way Gin had taught him, flat and sloppy and unremarkable. Then he shut the first. The floor went back to being linoleum. The walls went back to being walls. He was a young man on a kitchen floor in the dark, with a nosebleed and a book in his lap. Outside, a lantern on the balcony across the street knocked gently against its pole. And three hundred metres to the northeast, a man made of light was still holding a door with his back to the world. He had not turned around.
